doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Scoring the GoldenEye tank chase and a Bond brass moment
summary: He wrote the absurd tank chase cue for another composer's score, built excitement gradually, and matched the composer's devices; compares a recent Bond cue with Arturo Sandoval.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You were — there’s some marvelous interviews online that I have watched and I think you were describing a scene from a James Bond movie. And you used the word absurd. So I started thinking about adjectives and what goes through your head after you watch a sequence, even before you go to the piano or have a pencil in hand that might musicalize an adjective like absurd?

Well I mean taking for example that particular sequence, which I know is the GoldenEye tank chase. I had arranged and conducted the whole score for another composer. And when they did the — came to dub the film, they basically weren’t happy with what he’d written and they contacted me and said would you write something for this. And I said well I know what you want but I won’t do it unless the composer is happy, because I’m his arranger. And they phoned him and he — I think grudgingly — said yeah, I’m not going to do it, let him do it. So the case in point of the sequence was that it was totally absurd. I mean the scene is that James Bond chases a kidnapped woman through the streets of St. Petersburg in a tank, basically plowing through every building and bar and truck loaded with whatever, you know, water. I mean it’s insanity and totally unrealistic. But it also has to be exciting because it’s one of the big moments in the film plus there are mounting points of absurdity through the whole thing. So the first absurd thing is it bursts through the wall of the prison, the next absurd thing is it does something else, and then just when you think the whole thing’s climaxed it hits a statue and the statue lands on top of the tank as he’s driving it. So I mean you can’t peak within the first couple of minutes. You have to have excitement but then you have to build the excitement and build the excitement and then build it more. So it’s an interesting sequence because it’s one of those chases, and we had a similar thing in the new James Bond film that I wrote some brass arrangements for because there’s a whole scene in Cuba where there’s a big fight. But what they wanted to do was get the sort of salsa/Cuban element into the James Bond/Hans Zimmer milieu. So again it was an absurd moment, that you have to play on and build and stack up, and then we got Arturo Sandoval to play a solo and then we got the big brass section. But it’s still recognizably Hans Zimmer’s music you know.
That was going through my head there. How much do you have to be aware of what’s been written so far by another composer and try not to sound like an obvious change of arranger/composer.

Well particularly on that Bond thing I mentioned the scene, it’s the only thing I composed in the film. But because I’d orchestrated the rest of the film I knew tricks that the original composer had used in his score that subconsciously, I mean people probably wouldn’t have even realized that I used elements that he had used like certain percussive things like a triangle and — you know subtle touches that would link to what was written in the rest of the score. So you are always thinking in terms of that. You’re not going in like the bull in the china shop and going oh, I do it this way so that what you’ve done is going to stick out like a — I mean it stuck out anyway because there was no other brass in the whole film, and they hadn’t used the Bond theme really through the whole film. So suddenly to have a big brass James Bond moment probably stuck out from the rest of the score anyway but there’s nothing I could do about that, they wanted big James Bond so I gave it to them.
